### Materials

A single speech in Arabic delivered at a UN conference was selected as the experimental material. This speech was chosen because it reflects the UN’s standard practice of providing SI services into its six official languages, aligning with our focus on evaluating comprehension of interpreted content in professional settings. The original speech was interpreted into Chinese by professional UN interpreters, and the official video and audio recordings were publicly available on the UN website. To ensure experimental control, all participants across the three groups were exposed to identical speech content, which was then processed into three distinct delivery modes:

1.  Version A: Chinese auto-subtitling generated by an ASR system based on the Chinese SI audio.
2.  Version B: Chinese SI audio only, without subtitles.
3.  Version C: A combination of Chinese SI audio and Chinese automatic subtitles.

The speech content, pacing, and audiovisual quality were held constant across all three versions. Each version lasted exactly 3 minutes and 40 seconds. The use of a single speech across all experimental conditions was an intentional design choice aimed at maximizing internal validity. This design ensured that the only manipulated variable was the mode of delivery, while the linguistic content, discourse topic, and communicative context remained constant. Using a single speech allowed us to isolate the effects of delivery mode on cognitive effort and comprehension outcomes without introducing variability from message content or situational features.

To assess the participants’ comprehension of the speech in the target language, a multiple-choice test was developed in Simplified Chinese characters. The test consisted of 10 single-choice questions focused on factual recall, such as the speech’s main topics, numerical data, and named entities, to evaluate the participants’ immediate understanding of the content. An example of a question translated in English is as follows:

1.  “*What is the purpose of holding this summit?*
2.  A) To promote global economic recovery
3.  B) To emphasize national sovereignty and integrity
4.  C) To enhance economic cooperation among countries
5.  D) To reshape the multilateral system”
6.  Correct answer:
7.  D) This option directly reflects the central goal as stated in the speech: “reshape the multilateral system”.
8.  Distractor rationale:
9.  A) Reflects general UN themes related to development and recovery but does not align with the summit’s explicitly stated focus.
10.  B) Draws on the principle of respecting sovereignty mentioned in the speech but misrepresents it as the main purpose.
11.  C) Suggests international cooperation, a peripheral theme, but inaccurately elevates it to the summit’s core objective.

Each question was worth 10 points, with no partial credit awarded for incorrect or incomplete answers. As a result, the total comprehension score ranged from 0 to 100, with higher scores indicating better comprehension. To ensure the test’s validity and reliability, all questions and answer options were reviewed by a linguistics expert who specialized in translation and interpreting. This review ensured that the questions aligned with the speech content and that the wording of the answer options was clear, precise, and appropriate for assessing comprehension of the target language.

### Experimental procedure

A pilot test was conducted prior to the main study to ensure the feasibility of the experimental design and procedures. This included evaluating the functionality of video playback, the clarity of the instructions, and the timing of the comprehension test. Feedback from the pilot phase informed minor adjustments, including the rewording of comprehension questions to improve clarity and technical refinements to ensure the smooth functioning of all experimental components. One such revision involved replacing the original item **“Why was the summit important?”**, which invited subjective interpretation, with **“What is the purpose of holding this summit?”**, a fact-based question more directly anchored in the explicit linguistic content of the source text. The pilot confirmed the feasibility of the materials and procedures for the main experiment. Accordingly, the formal study adopted the validated setup—including standardized video playback procedures—and was conducted in a controlled lab environment to ensure consistency and data reliability.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of three experimental conditions—SI, automatic subtitles, or dual-modality (SI + automatic subtitles)—using a computer-generated randomization sequence. Each participant experienced only one modality condition and viewed the same stimulus video in a fixed order, followed by comprehension questions. Random allocation was employed to control for potential between-group variation unrelated to the experimental treatment.

Each participant selected a session time based on their availability and was informed in advance that they would receive a HK$50 gift card as compensation. Based on each participant’s selected schedule, the research team reserved the lab and ensured the appropriate condition materials were prepared. To minimize bias, participants were explicitly instructed not to discuss their experiences or the test content with one another until all sessions were completed.

Upon arrival, the participant was provided with a consent form to read and sign, ensuring ethical compliance with the study protocol. Following this, the participant was briefed on the experimental procedure and introduced to the wireless EEG device, which was used to monitor their cognitive activity. Each experimental session was conducted individually. A trained research assistant assisted the participant in correctly positioning the wireless EEG headset and ensured that 100% contact quality was achieved before proceeding with the task.

Once the EEG setup and baseline signal confirmation were complete, the participant was seated at an individual station and the video presentation commenced. During the video viewing, researchers monitored the participant from a separate room to ensure uninterrupted EEG data collection and to quickly address any technical issues. The environment was carefully controlled to eliminate distractions, such as noise or external interference, ensuring consistent testing conditions for each participant.

To maintain consistency, the video could not be paused or replayed during the experiment. The comprehension questions were only accessible after the video had ended, to ensure that the participant relied solely on the presented material. [Fig 2](#pone-0330692-g002) presents the participant wearing the EEG device while watching the video material.

## Results

### Content comprehension

After all participants completed the experiments, their comprehension scores were collected and processed for statistical analysis. To compare comprehension scores across the three groups, the Kruskal-Wallis test was employed. The analysis yielded an **H** statistic of 0.407 (**df** = 2, **p** = 0.816). As **p** **\>** 0.05, the null hypothesis of equal distributions across groups was not rejected. This result indicates that there were no statistically significant differences in comprehension scores among the three groups.

Descriptive statistics ([Table 2](#pone-0330692-t002)) show a gradual increase in mean scores: Group A (automatic subtitles) scored 70.00, Group B (SI) scored 74.00, and Group C (dual-modality) scored 75.33. Although the differences were statistically non-significant, this incremental pattern suggests potential benefits of dual-modality delivery for comprehension.

Group A exhibited the highest variability (*SD* = 23.30), with scores ranging from 20 to 100, compared to narrower ranges in Group B (40–100) and Group C (30–100). Notably, all groups included participants achieving perfect scores (100), indicating that each modality could support optimal comprehension under favorable conditions. Group C, however, combined the highest mean score with a relatively homogeneous distribution (*SD* = 18.85), suggesting enhanced stability in information processing.

Participants’ neurological responses to three distinct content delivery modes were investigated through analysis of brain activity patterns across participant groups. ### Viewing experience

Regarding the viewing experience, [Fig 4](#pone-0330692-g004) illustrates the hierarchical pattern of beta waves associated with active cognitive processing, problem-solving, and alertness, providing insights into the participants’ engagement levels and potential stress responses \[[60](#pone.0330692.ref060),[62](#pone.0330692.ref062)\]. Elevated beta waves activity is generally correlated with excessive levels may indicate anxiety or stress \[[60](#pone.0330692.ref060),[62](#pone.0330692.ref062)\]. Results show that Group A exhibited the highest beta band activation, indicating the highest stress level, followed by Group B, with Group C showing the lowest level of stress.

In addition to the raw EEG data, which were subsequently drawn as a topographic brain activity heatmap, the Emotiv Pro Suite software package was used to obtain stress values for the participants from the EEG devices while watching the 220-second conference video. ## Discussion

### How do automatic subtitles compare to SI in facilitating content comprehension for viewers?

The experimental results revealed that the mode of delivery of translated information across the three groups did not significantly impact viewers’ comprehension scores. This aligns with findings by Szarkowska et al. \[[19](#pone.0330692.ref019)\], who observed that the absence of audio input had only a modest effect on comprehension when subtitles were available. In addition, Liao et al. \[[63](#pone.0330692.ref063)\] found that when participants watched videos with subtitles but without accompanying audio, comprehension scores remained similar to those of participants who had access to both modalities. Other studies have further supported this observation, finding that even the non-syntactic segmentation of subtitles (i.e., splitting sentences at unnatural points) does not negatively impact viewers’ comprehension \[[64](#pone.0330692.ref064),[65](#pone.0330692.ref065)\].

While our statistical analysis revealed only minor differences in comprehension scores across experimental conditions, the group exposed to a combination of automatic subtitles and SI achieved the highest average comprehension scores. This finding highlights the potential of multimodal translation delivery to enhance participants’ understanding \[[19](#pone.0330692.ref019)\]. By distributing information across auditory and visual channels, the dual-modality approach allows participants to process content more efficiently, as cognitive resources can be shared between modalities, reducing the strain on any single processing channel.

This distribution aligns with the cognitive theory of multimedia learning \[[66](#pone.0330692.ref066),[67](#pone.0330692.ref067)\], which suggests that synchronizing corresponding visual and auditory material reduces cognitive load. Subtitles can clarify ambiguous or unfamiliar auditory input, while auditory content provides additional context or emotional nuance that subtitles alone may not fully convey \[[19](#pone.0330692.ref019)\]. The complementary nature of these modalities enhances understanding while minimizing the risk of cognitive overload, particularly in complex or fast-paced content. Consequently, multimodal delivery systems, such as the combination of automatic subtitles and SI, represent an effective and accessible strategy to support participants’ comprehension, especially in multilingual or cognitively demanding environments.

### What differences in cognitive demands do automatic subtitles and SI impose on viewers?

The experimental findings yielded important insights into cognitive effort during conference content processing across the three experimental groups. Analysis of EEG topographic brain activity indicated significant variations in cognitive effort between the SI (listening) and automatic subtitles (reading) conditions, offering valuable theoretical and practical implications.

The theta waves measurements demonstrated a hierarchical pattern of cognitive demand: Group B (SI only) exhibited the highest theta power, followed by Group A (automatic subtitles only), while Group C (combined SI and automatic subtitles) showed the lowest level. This finding is particularly relevant to conference interpreting, as conference attendees relying on translation services experience varying levels of cognitive load depending on the modality through which they receive translated information. The heightened cognitive effort in the SI-only condition suggests additional mental resources were needed for participants to comprehend by processing only auditory information while those listened to SI likely due to the mental effort required to process and comprehend auditory input in real time. In contrast, attendees using automatic subtitles only showed lower cognitive demand, as reading visual text may involve a less resource-intensive processing pathway. Most notably, attendees who had access to both SI and auto-subtitles, exhibited the lowest theta power, indicating reduced cognitive strain when provided with multimodal inputs. The minimal cognitive effort observed for Group C finds robust theoretical support from the bilingual dual-coding theory \[[68](#pone.0330692.ref068)\] that suggests memory performance improves when information is processed through multiple channels, in our case the visual and audio channels. These findings extend beyond simple cognitive load measurement, suggesting that the traditional reliance on audio-only SI may not fully optimize audience comprehension and engagement.

The comparison of Groups A and B reveals an interesting deviation from conventional assumptions that watching subtitle videos without corresponding audio would increase cognitive load as viewers use metacognitive strategies to adjust their visual processing to maintain comprehension \[[19](#pone.0330692.ref019),[69](#pone.0330692.ref069)\]. Audio input is transient and sequential, while visual input is often static and simultaneous, allowing viewers to process information at their own pace and revisit it as needed. Our finding may reflect the experimental setting, which simulated a conference setting where attendees typically listen to speakers for various purposes. In this context, participants were motivated to understand the experimental material, whether through auto-subtitles, SI, or a combination of both, potentially requiring additional cognitive resources for comprehension and retention. Our findings suggest that the professional context significantly may influence how different modalities affect cognitive processing.

arguments.message:
FULL PREMISE RED-TEAM

BOTTOM LINE: Do not position this as an autonomous live-fact-checking PWA with automatic dual displays. The smallest credible product is a presentation safety copilot: pre-verified evidence playlist + private live research inbox + optional presenter-approved public receipts. The current design puts its most visible promise on its least reliable path. There is a hard demo dilemma: strict safety gates make the public evidence screen frequently empty (looks broken); forcing something to appear in five seconds makes it unsafe (looks impressive until it is wrong).

A. PWA / MULTI-DISPLAY ATTACK
- “PWA” is packaging, installability, and service-worker capability; it does not grant window-placement, popup, fullscreen, microphone, or multi-screen privileges. Automatic placement is a separate Window Management API enhancement.
- MDN documents one user gesture per `window.open()`, popup-blocker `null`, browser correction of requested coordinates, and user/extension control over tab-vs-window behavior. Fullscreen requires transient activation in the target document and can reject. This is not a deterministic stage launcher.
- Security’s separate-origin decision intentionally removes direct opener/BroadcastChannel coordination. Therefore the product is actually a cloud-synchronized two-client application; WSS availability becomes part of even nearby-screen reliability.
- Mirror and extend are not one architecture. Mirror’s safe path is a second authenticated device; extend’s baseline is manual window placement. If a single behavior is needed, use stage-only presentation PC + phone/tablet console in BOTH modes. Window Management then becomes convenience, not topology logic.
- Additional contradiction: a QR shown on a “private setup console” becomes public the moment Windows mirroring begins. Pair before projection starts, or never show setup/QR on the presentation PC after mirroring.
- If “automatic projector placement with no local stage click” is contractual, use a tiny signed Windows/Electron launcher or PowerPoint add-in. A PWA-alone promise is indefensible. If native software is out, rename the feature “guided multi-display setup on Chromium desktop; manual placement elsewhere.”

Evidence: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window_Management_API ; https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/open ; https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Element/requestFullscreen

B. FIVE-SECOND LIVE WEB SEARCH ATTACK
- Five seconds measures transport/computation, not truth. Real-world verification requires claim decomposition, raw web retrieval, fine-grained evidence retrieval, summarization, and judgment. NAACL 2024’s realistic pipeline says its output can assist fact-checkers even when it does not reflect a complete evidence set. That is a research assistant, not a publication oracle.
- Searching can actively hurt: Nature’s experiments found online search used to evaluate misinformation can move users into “data voids” with low-quality corroborating sources. A speed target biases toward fast/indexable sources, not primary/current/complete sources.
- Google Fact Check Tools searches existing ClaimReview records; it neither creates a fresh original-source verification nor guarantees current coverage. Search snippets are relevance hints, not proof.
- Live origins add WAF/paywall/JS-render/redirect/timeout/date ambiguity; numbers and named entities are exactly where Korean STT and source reconciliation are brittle. A hard five-second deadline systematically abstains on the claims most worth checking.
- Separate the clocks: <=5s p95 for a PRIVATE candidate; no time promise for verified publication. Public approval->render may have a sub-500ms target. Timeout must become HOLD/NO RESULT, never “best available.”

Evidence: https://aclanthology.org/2024.naacl-long.196/ ; https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06883-y ; https://developers.google.com/fact-check/tools/api/reference/rest/

C. EXTRA EVIDENCE SCREEN ATTACK
- The “extra screen improves presentations” premise is unproven. Split-attention research warns that related information on spatially separate visual sources forces gaze switching and working-memory integration. This evidence is analogous rather than a direct test of this exact product, which is why the product must run its own experiment.
- At <=3 new cards every five seconds, the audience cannot both follow the speaker/slide and read source/claim/date/status. Cards will either be ignored, or steal attention from the argument they are meant to support.
- Public labels such as SUPPORTED can create automation authority and false certainty. A card that appears, then becomes STALE/SUPERSEDED, may amplify doubt rather than calibrate it.
- Accessibility can justify captions or integrated labels, but does not justify a separate dynamic evidence wall. A 2025 controlled subtitle/SI study found delivery mode effects are context-dependent and no statistically significant comprehension difference across its three groups; extrapolation to evidence cards would be invalid.
- Better hypothesis: evidence should be audience-PULL, not system-PUSH. Show one unobtrusive source badge integrated with the current slide; let audience scan a QR for the full timestamped evidence ledger during/after the talk.

Evidence: https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/cambridge-handbook-of-multimedia-learning/splitattention-principle-in-multimedia-learning/194CBCD1A3C911116CCB5F403AC7E415 ; https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0330692

D. DEMO-KILLING FAILURE PRE-MORTEM
P0 — immediate visible failure:
1. Popup blocked or stage opens as a tab/wrong monitor; presenter exposes console while fixing it.
2. Stage needs its own fullscreen gesture; browser chrome remains visible.
3. Windows is in Duplicate, not Extend; private setup/console/QR is projected.
4. Wrong/denied microphone, Bluetooth profile switch, room echo/noise; STT never finalizes or corrupts names/numbers.
5. Venue Wi-Fi/captive portal/firewall/cold backend breaks WSS or search. Public stage freezes/reconnects.
6. Strict verifier produces no eligible card; promised “AI evidence screen” stays empty.

P1 — reputational/security failure:
7. A fast but low-quality corroborating page wins; wrong claim is labeled SUPPORTED.
8. Original page is blocked/paywalled/dynamic; snippet masquerades as evidence.
9. Presenter is speaking and ignores approval queue; card expires or appears after slide change.
10. Source/ACL/revision changes between retrieval and approval; stale private content becomes public.
11. Logged-out phone hits SSO/MFA during QR pairing; setup stalls in front of the room.
12. Privacy/right/DLP false negative leaks personal/internal data; false positive suppresses every interesting card.

P2 — reliability erosion:
13. Stage and console run different service-worker/app protocol versions.
14. Reconnect applies duplicate relative commands or stale controller frames.
15. Projector scaling makes citations illegible; audience watches the wrong screen.
16. Hot-plug/display mode change exits fullscreen or leaves topology assumptions stale.
17. Browser WebSocket has no backpressure; event bursts/slow display create lag unless state is coalesced.

E. SIMPLER, MORE RELIABLE ALTERNATIVES
1. RECOMMENDED MVP — Evidence Playlist: upload-time retrieval, rights/privacy review, and human approval create immutable cards tied to slide IDs and speaker cue phrases. Live STT only MATCHES a pre-approved card. This easily meets five seconds without live epistemology.
2. Backstage Live Research: live web search may generate private presenter/team candidates. Nothing from this path is promised publicly during the talk. Accepted items enter the post-talk evidence ledger.
3. Audience Receipt, not Evidence Wall: integrate a one-line source badge or QR into the current stage. Full citations, conflicts, and updates live on a pull-based mobile page and post-session report.
4. Universal Remote Topology: presentation PC always runs Audience Stage only; presenter always uses phone/tablet console. Extended-screen desktop console is optional convenience. This removes privacy behavior differences between mirror/extend and makes the demo identical everywhere.
5. Native assist only if necessary: a minimal Windows launcher owns display enumeration/window placement/fullscreen. Keep content/session UI web-based. Do not build native unless the auto-placement promise survives experiments.
6. Q&A mode: allow 15–30 seconds for live evidence lookup after a question, with an explicit “researching / insufficient evidence” state. This is more useful and more honest than interrupting the prepared talk every five seconds.

F. BOUNDED EXPERIMENTS WITH GO/NO-GO GATES
1. Display setup gauntlet — 48 fresh starts: Chrome/Edge x Extend/Duplicate x clean/returning profile x popup allowed/blocked, three repeats, real Windows projector. GO automatic-setup copy only if supported-matrix success >=95%, p95 ready <=60s, zero private pixels on stage, and manual fallback

arguments.message:
FULL RED-TEAM VERDICT

Bottom line: do not make “live public fact-checking on a PWA evidence screen” the MVP center. The dependable and valuable core is a presenter copilot: rehearsed deck intelligence, private live cues, pre-approved evidence, and post-session audit. Public live web cards should remain an experiment until they beat a static baseline on comprehension without increasing distraction or error.

A. PWA/multi-display premise
- PWA installation is packaging, not capability. It grants no extra screen placement, fullscreen, popup, microphone, or connectivity privilege.
- The actual dependable baseline is ordinary browser windows: user opens one stage, drags it, clicks fullscreen. Window Management is a Chromium-desktop enhancement; getScreenDetails can be denied; window.open can return null, positions are clamped, each new window needs a gesture; cross-origin stage needs its own fullscreen gesture.
- Mirror detection is particularly treacherous: mirrored output is not a distinct screen to the API, and the app cannot prove OBS/screen sharing/HDMI topology. Calling privacy “guaranteed” is false.
- Therefore copy must be: “guided dual-display setup; automatic placement on supported Chromium desktops.” If “automatic on all Windows presentation machines” is required, PWA-alone fails; use an Electron/native launcher only for deployment-controlled venues, or accept guided manual setup.

B. Five-second live-web premise
- Five seconds can buy plausible retrieval, not trustworthy verification. Real-world claim checking is multi-stage: claim decomposition, raw retrieval, fine evidence retrieval, summarization, judgment. NAACL 2024 explicitly describes a five-component realistic pipeline and says even reliable summaries may not be complete evidence sets: https://aclanthology.org/2024.naacl-long.196/
- Search can actively worsen judgment. Nature reported that searching to evaluate misinformation can land users in “data voids” containing corroboration from low-quality sources: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06883-y
- Google Fact Check API only searches previously published ClaimReview material; it cannot verify a novel utterance, and Google does not create/endorse those checks: https://developers.google.com/fact-check/tools/api/reference/rest/
- Snippets, generated URLs, or a semantic-match score must never become “SUPPORTED.” The bottleneck is source/claim fit, temporal validity, units/entities, source authority, rights/privacy/ACL—not model inference time.
- Correct SLA: p95 final-utterance -> PRIVATE eligible candidate <=5s, with timeout -> no card. Measure STT endpointing separately. Public approval/render is a separate SLO. Hard or novel claims should often yield zero results; abstention is success.
- Useful alternative: upload-time evidence compilation plus live retrieval only from the frozen approved bundle. External web search runs asynchronously into presenter-only “needs review,” or during Q&A when a deliberate pause exists.

C. Audience evidence-screen premise
- There is no established benefit merely from adding another public screen. Split-attention theory warns against requiring people to integrate spatially separated sources; a meta-analysis and handbook literature support integrating rather than separating related representations: https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/cambridge-handbook-of-multimedia-learning/splitattention-principle-in-multimedia-learning/194CBCD1A3C911116CCB5F403AC7E415
- Evidence cards arrive after the sentence, pull gaze away from the speaker/current slide, may expire before reading, and can publicly amplify a false or contentious claim. Three cards every five seconds is a notification machine, not a presentation aid.
- Contrary nuance: extra visual layers can help accessibility when complementary and synchronized. A 2025 PLOS experiment found no significant comprehension difference between subtitles, interpreting, and both, though combined mode reduced measured effort/stress in that narrow multilingual setup: https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0330692 . This does NOT generalize to unrelated evidence cards; it argues for captions/number-name reinforcement before an auxiliary fact stream.
- Safer public design: one integrated, presenter-invoked “evidence moment,” replacing or occupying a reserved region of the current slide—not a continuously mutating second canvas. Default private; public only on explicit cue. After talk, offer QR-accessible evidence ledger for depth.

D. Demo killers, ranked
P0: projector mirrors private console because topology assumption is wrong; mic permission denied/wrong device; popup blocked; stage opens as tab/on wrong screen; audience stage cannot fullscreen remotely; venue Wi-Fi/portal/API key/quota outage; Korean STT corrupts a number/name and searches the wrong claim; public card asserts stale/contradictory evidence; operator misses approval while speaking; stale card appears after slide change; source is paywalled/JS-only/robots-blocked; WSS reconnect shows divergent revision.
P1: browser update/service-worker version skew between windows; phone pairing/login delay; battery/lock/background throttling; duplicate relative next after reconnect; external search latency tail; malicious page prompt-injects verifier; rights/license forbids displaying image; accessibility failure from unreadable/rapid updates; Windows notification or browser chrome leaks on projector.
P2: visual polish defects, optional WebRTC failure, install prompt absence. These matter far less than safe manual recovery.

E. Simpler product ladder
1) MVP “Presenter Copilot”: existing slide deck remains authoritative; private phone/laptop console shows notes, timing, Q&A prompts, and upload-time evidence. Public projector stays unchanged. No multi-display automation needed.
2) “Evidence Button”: pre-approved card deck, presenter manually invokes a card; stage receives immutable public DTO. Works offline after prefetch and is demo-safe.
3) “Live Assist”: streaming STT suggests private queries/candidates from approved corpus; no public auto-publish.
4) “Live Web Beta”: external sources, private-only, logs failures/abstentions.
5) Only after evidence: public live cards and Chromium auto-placement. Electron launcher is optional for controlled Windows fleets, not a default architecture.

F. Bounded experiments / go-no-go
E1 Setup reliability: 30 cold starts across 3 Windows versions x Chrome/Edge/Firefox x extend/mirror x popup allowed/blocked; novice gets 90s. GO if >=95% reach correct public-only stage without facilitator and zero private leaks; otherwise manual setup is the only supported contract.
E2 Recovery chaos: during 20 talks inject Wi-Fi loss, WSS drop, phone lock, screen hotplug, fullscreen exit, API timeout. GO if slide control remains locally usable, audience sees a safe holding/current slide, recovery <10s p95, zero duplicate commands/private bytes.
E3 Korean STT: 200 target utterances with names, dates, money, units, code-switching, venue noise. Gate on semantic claim accuracy, not WER. GO live search only if >=95% key entity/number/unit correctness or those errors are detected and suppressed.
E4 Verification: 300 utterances (supported/contradictory/unverifiable, time-sensitive, multi-hop). Blind human gold labels. GO if public-eligible precision >=99%, false-support <=1%, and abstention is uncapped; latency p95 <=5s only among eligible candidates. No cherry-picked demo scripts.
E5 Audience value: randomized crossover, >=60 audience members, same talk: no cards vs presenter-invoked integrated cards vs automatic second screen. Measure delayed comprehension, claim-source calibration, speaker recall, gaze switches, distraction, trust. Ship public screen only if it materially improves comprehension/calibration and does not worsen speaker recall/distraction; subjective “looks impressive” is not enough.
E6 Presenter load: >=12 presenters, rehearsal + live. Measure missed cues, approval time, speech disfluency, NASA-TLX, wrong approvals. GO if evidence controls do not worsen delivery and >=90% approvals complete without stopping speech; otherwise assign a producer role or make cards pre-approved/manual.
E7 Security: audience-role byte capture, QR race, stale-controller command, ACL revoked between retrieval/publish, malicious source prompt. GO requires zero private canary bytes, one winner per pairing, all stale/unauthorized publishes denied.
E8 Demo dress rehearsal: ten consecutive end-to-end runs on venue hardware/network with fresh profiles and no engineer intervention. One P0 failure resets the count.

Decision rule: if E4 or E5 fails, kill public live evidence—not the whole product. Preserve Presenter Copilot + pre-approved Evidence Button, which captures most value with a fraction of the epistemic and platform risk.

## EXPAND
- LEAD: Compare an even more radical “no auxiliary screen” design: subtle evidence markers embedded in the main slide plus a post-talk evidence ledger.
- LEAD: Test whether the actual buyer values trust/audit more than spectacle; procurement may prefer an exportable source ledger over live cards.
- LEAD: Define explicit kill metrics now so the team cannot rationalize a flashy but harmful second screen after building it.
- DEAD END: Treating PWA installation as a way around browser permissions or popup/fullscreen rules is refuted by the platform model.
